reasons: I could not run the tests in this session.
Coverage is detailed for one line and one substation naming style, but other utilities use different names.

terms.meaning: a simplified drawing that places parts by their names and rough roles, not by surveyed positions.
the work breakdown structure location of an activity, written as slash-separated folder names.
a main metal conductor in a substation that collects power from several circuits.
a column of switching equipment in a substation that connects one circuit to the bus.
a pole or frame that holds a line at its end, where it stops at the yard.
the distance between two supporting structures along a line.
the wire that carries electricity along a line.
a capacitor voltage transformer, a device that measures high voltage on a line.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Setup and sample names
sections.what: Imports the layout functions and the phase labels, and sets sample line and yard names used across the tests.
sections.why: Keeps the example names in one place so every test uses the same realistic schedule text.
sections.watch_out: The names must match the patterns the layout code looks for, so editing them can silently change test meaning.

sections.name: paths
sections.title: Sample line and yard paths
sections.what: Builds a list of activity paths for three line structures, each with a foundation, a conductor, a fiber ground wire, and a yard with buses, rungs, breakers, switches, a control house and its panel.
sections.why: Provides one realistic site that the main layout tests share.
sections.watch_out: Structure numbering in this list sets the expected order of poles, so changing the numbers changes the expected spacing.

sections.name: test_line_structures_form_an_ordered_corridor_with_conductors_between_poles
sections.title: Line poles form an ordered corridor
sections.what: Checks that the three poles sit on the ground in a straight line at equal spacing, with the last pole nearest the yard. It also checks that the foundation sits at the second pole, the conductor runs from the far pole into the substation, and the fiber wire sits above the conductor.
sections.why: Likely reason: the numbering runs toward the yard, so the drawing must show the poles in that order, not randomly.
sections.watch_out: Pole order depends on the name North Spa in the line name, so renaming the line changes the expected direction.

sections.name: test_substation_buses_are_parallel_rows_with_bays_between_them
sections.title: Buses run in parallel with bays between
sections.what: Checks that bus one and bus two are separate rows, with bus one to the north and bus two to the south, that all bus parts are bus supports, that the bays sit between the rows at one shared position, and that the breaker, control building and panel are placed correctly. It also checks that the nearest pole stays outside the yard.
sections.why: Likely reason: a real substation has parallel bus rows with equipment between them, and the drawing must not overlap the yard.
sections.watch_out: The comments say single-phase supports have their own phase, so their z positions spread out, which tests depend on.

sections.name: test_pole_foundation_and_site_preparation_sit_at_ground_level
sections.title: Pole foundation and site ground level
sections.what: Checks that a pole is shown as a pole in the structural phase, its foundation sits at a height of 0.3 in the foundation phase, and the enabling phase shows a slab.
sections.why: Likely reason: foundations and site preparation should sit at ground level so the drawing shows them in the right phase.
sections.watch_out: The 0.3 height is a fixed value, so changing the foundation depth rule will fail this test.

sections.name: test_schedules_without_line_or_substation_keep_generic_packing
sections.title: Schedules without line or substation stay generic
sections.what: Checks that a schedule for an ordinary building returns an empty layout, so the generic packing is used instead.
sections.why: Likely reason: the line and substation rules should not affect unrelated building schedules.
sections.watch_out: If the layout starts placing ordinary building names, this test will catch it.

sections.name: _ends
sections.title: Helper for conductor ends
sections.what: Works out the two end points of a placed item from its width and rotation, so the tests can compare where a line really ends.
sections.why: Lets tests check whether a tie span touches the terminal and the pole, without repeating the geometry in each test.
sections.watch_out: The rotation and half-width math must match how the layout stores items, or the end points will be wrong.

sections.name: _close
sections.title: Helper for matching positions
sections.what: Compares two two-number positions and says whether they match within a very small tolerance.
sections.why: Floating point numbers are rarely exact, so a tolerance is needed for position checks.
sections.watch_out: The tolerance is tiny, so a slightly larger rounding change could make checks fail.

sections.name: test_line_is_strung_into_its_named_terminal_in_the_substation
sections.title: Line ties into its named terminal
sections.what: Checks that a terminal named Line work Alpha becomes a dead-end structure, that a tie span runs from that terminal to the nearest pole, that the line leaves toward the side the terminal faces, and that the conductor covers only pole-to-pole spans when a tie activity exists. A terminal with no line in the schedule stays a dead end in its bay.
sections.why: Likely reason: the tie span is the only link between the line and the yard, so it must join the right structures.
sections.watch_out: The tie activity name must contain the phrase Tie to North Spa sub, or the link is not found.

sections.name: test_structures_that_are_wbs_leaves_still_form_a_corridor
sections.title: Wbs leaf structures still form a corridor
sections.what: Checks that structures named directly under the structures folder, such as Dead End 1, Structure 2 or ESSS 1, still become poles in a corridor, with the conductor placed as an overhead line.
sections.why: Some schedules put activities directly under structure names instead of under a sub-folder, and the drawing must still show them.
sections.watch_out: Each structure must get a unique position, so a change to number parsing can make two structures overlap.

sections.name: test_area_level_substation_groups_form_a_real_yard
sections.title: Area-level substation groups form a yard
sections.what: Checks that yard groups named only as bus and rung areas, with placeholder leaves, still become a bus row pair, switch bays in separate columns, a control building and a slab. It also checks that the bus foundation is a pad row.
sections.why: Likely reason: some schedules stop at area level, and the drawing should still show a usable yard.
sections.watch_out: The placeholder name No custom property is treated as empty, so changing that placeholder changes which items are grouped.

sections.name: test_activity_names_split_area_level_substation_wbs_into_items
sections.title: Activity names split yard areas into items
sections.what: Checks that the function item_group_path turns a detailed activity name into a named equipment item inside its area, such as Breaker 2.1 or Line work Alpha with a Line trap or Line switch part. It also checks that generic names and paths outside a substation stay unchanged.
sections.why: Likely reason: area-level paths hide individual equipment, so splitting them by name lets each piece be drawn separately.
sections.watch_out: The matching is by name text, so a new equipment name will stay grouped at area level until a rule is added.

sections.name: test_item_level_substation_builds_each_named_piece_of_equipment
sections.title: Each named equipment item is built
sections.what: Checks that every named item in a detailed substation, including bus supports, bus tubes, breakers, disconnect switches, dead-end structures, panels, ground grid, fencing and lightning masts, gets its own shape type. It also checks the order of switches and breakers along a rung, the order of line terminal parts from the bus outward, and that panels stand inside the control house shell.
sections.why: Likely reason: the detailed view is only useful if each piece is recognized and placed in its real order.
sections.watch_out: The order checks depend on the z positions, so a change to spacing or direction rules can flip the expected order.

summary: Checks the schematic site layout: where poles, conductors, buses, breakers, switches, control buildings and other substation parts are placed, and how line work connects to the yard.
purpose: Makes sure the simplified 3D site drawing shows a plausible line corridor and yard from the activity names in a schedule.
why: Likely reason: the layout is built from text names alone, so these tests lock in the placement rules that give the drawing a believable structure.
how: A helper returns a fixed list of activity paths for a line and substation. Tests call the layout function and check primitive shapes, positions, spacing, and how the conductor and tie span meet the terminal. Other tests cover area-level yards, item-level equipment names and grouping of activity names into items.
inputs: Lists of WBS path strings built inside the test file.
outputs: Pass or fail results. The layout function returns positions and shape types for each path.
risks: The layout depends on exact name patterns such as Erect Poles, Bus 1 and Rung 2. A schedule with different naming may fall back to generic packing or lose parts silently.
debug: If a layout test fails, print the layout dictionary for the failing paths and compare names with the patterns in the layout code. Check the spacing constants first when positions are off.
